## Where the trace goes dark, and what still shows {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

**The case:** a ransom trace reaches a transaction that breaks its links, and the agent asks where the money went. A trace that simply stops names no one, so today is what to say at the stop: where it ends, why, and what the ledger still shows.

**The last lesson ended** on confidence: every label carries a source and a confidence word. Today uses that habit on the tools built to break the clustering clues. Three parts:

1. **CoinJoin:** one transaction that several owners build together, so co-spending no longer means one owner.
2. **Mixers, habits and who runs them:** a service that pays out other coins, and what users do that links a deposit to a withdrawal.
3. **The limits-of-tracing note:** how you write the stop, so the stop is a finding.

**By the end:** given a trace that reaches a CoinJoin or a mixer, say where it stops, why, what still shows past the stop, and how sure you are (High, Moderate or Low).

**The point to earn:** a CoinJoin or a mixer cuts the clustering clues, but it does not erase the ledger. What went in, what came out and what users did around the mix are still on it [@svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026; @wang_zkpmixers_2023].

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide opens the lesson with a case and a question: a ransom trace reaches a transaction that breaks its links, and the agent asks where the money went. It matters here because the last lesson ended on a confidence word for every label, and the tools in this lesson are built to defeat the clues those words rest on. Emphasize the objective: the practice and the review come back to it.

**Key Points**
- Students arrive knowing two things. The clustering lesson taught co-spending (inputs spent together share an owner) and change, and the attribution lesson taught that every label and link carries a source and a confidence word.
- A CoinJoin or a mixer defeats those clues on purpose. Part 1 shows a CoinJoin, part 2 a mixer and the habits that still link a deposit to a withdrawal, and part 3 turns both into the written note the afternoon lab asks for.
- The point is a claim to earn, not one to assume. The ledger still records the inputs, the outputs and the users' behavior around the mix, so "the trace stops here" is a finding as long as it says why and what still shows.
- Privacy coins (Monero, Zcash) come in the next lesson, not this one.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the case and leave the agent's question open; the lesson answers it.
2. Read the link back to the last lesson, then name the three parts.
3. Read the objective aloud. Each of the first two parts ends with a check every student answers, and the close asks the objective again.
4. Time plan, 50 minutes: opening 3, part 1 13, part 2 13, part 3 14, close 7. The optional five-minute lab on the "Before and after the mix" slide is outside the plan: run it only with time in hand.

**Sources**
- @svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026
- @wang_zkpmixers_2023

:::

## A CoinJoin is many owners in one transaction {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

- **The heuristic it breaks:** the clustering lesson read inputs spent together as one owner (co-spending). A CoinJoin is one transaction that several users build and each sign for their own inputs [@gmaxwell_coinjoinbitcoinprivacy_2013].
- **The cost of missing it:** treating a CoinJoin's inputs as one wallet makes clustering "erroneously merge unrelated address groups" [@svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026, p. 557].
- **Anonymity set:** the equal outputs a coin could have become. The larger the set, the weaker any guess.
- **Analyst move:** mark the transaction as a CoinJoin and do not cluster across it.

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}

```{dot}
//| echo: false
//| fig-height: 1.8
digraph CoinJoinTx {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent", splines=ortho, nodesep=0.15, ranksep=0.4];
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=8];
  A_in [label="User A", fillcolor="#E6F7FF"];
  B_in [label="User B", fillcolor="#FFF5CC"];
  C_in [label="User C", fillcolor="#E8F5E9"];
  TX [label="CoinJoin", shape=ellipse, fillcolor="#ffdddd"];
  subgraph cluster_outs {
    label="Anonymity set";
    style=dashed;
    fontname="Helvetica";
    fontsize=9;
    Out1 [label="0.1"];
    Out2 [label="0.1"];
    Out3 [label="0.1"];
  }
  {A_in, B_in, C_in} -> TX -> {Out1, Out2, Out3};
}
```

:::
::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide defines CoinJoin as the known false positive of the co-spend heuristic. It matters here because a missed CoinJoin merges strangers into one cluster, and every later hop inherits the error. Emphasize that the move is to stop clustering, not to guess.

**Key Points**
- The opening named CoinJoin as the first thing that breaks co-spending; this slide shows how. Gregory Maxwell proposed CoinJoin in 2013: users combine their payments into one transaction, each signing only their own inputs.
- Svenda et al. warn that missing a CoinJoin makes clustering merge unrelated address groups.
- Anonymity set: the outputs among which one user's coin is hidden; three here, often far more.
- The diagram's 0.1 outputs are illustrative.

**Walkthrough**
1. Point at the three inputs: three owners, one transaction.
2. Ask: if you applied the co-spend heuristic here, what would your cluster contain? (Users A, B and C as one wallet: wrong.)

**Sources**
- @gmaxwell_coinjoinbitcoinprivacy_2013
- @svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026

:::

## Repeated equal amounts mark a CoinJoin {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** the three main designs each leave a shape you can spot; researchers detected Wasabi 1.x and Samourai CoinJoins with "> 99%" accuracy [@stutz_adoptionprivacycoinjoin_2022].

::: {style="font-size: .8em;"}

| Design | Shape on the chain | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wasabi 1.x | Many outputs of about 0.1 BTC each; from 2019 also set multiples such as 0.2, 0.4 and 0.8 BTC | [@svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026, sec. 2.1] |
| Wasabi 2.x (WabiSabi) | Many inputs and outputs; "arbitrary output denominations", so look for amounts that repeat, not one size | [@svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026, sec. 2.1] |
| Samourai Whirlpool | 5 inputs by 5 outputs, later up to 8 by 8, all one pool size: 0.001, 0.01, 0.05 or 0.5 BTC | [@svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026, sec. 2.1] |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,50,28]"}

:::

- **Scale:** these three designs have mixed more than 391,000 BTC since 2018 [@svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026] [31 Oct 2026]{.asof}.
- **For the analyst:** many outputs of one repeated amount in one transaction is a CoinJoin until shown otherwise.

**Ask:** one input of a Whirlpool round is in your ransom cluster. Which output is the ransom's now?

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide shows that CoinJoins are easy to recognize: their equal outputs are the point of the design. It matters here because recognizing one is the analyst's first move, and the shapes differ by wallet. Emphasize that recognizing a CoinJoin is easy; seeing through it is not.

**Key Points**
- Wasabi 1.x: one denomination of about 0.1 BTC at its 2018 release; version 1.1.0 (2019) added set multiples such as 0.2, 0.4 and 0.8 BTC, so a round shows a few fixed sizes, each repeated.
- Wasabi 2.x: WabiSabi allows many denominations, so there is no single size; the tell is many inputs and outputs with several amounts each repeated. The title says "repeated equal amounts" for that reason.
- Whirlpool: small fixed pools (5x5, later 8x8) at 0.001, 0.01, 0.05 or 0.5 BTC.
- Stütz et al. detected 30,251 Wasabi and 223,597 Samourai CoinJoins with highly accurate (> 99%) algorithms.
- Svenda et al. count more than 391,000 BTC mixed by the three designs since 2018.
- A coordinator is the server that gathers users into each round; the coordinator is what 2024's enforcement ended (later slide).

**Walkthrough**
1. Draw a Whirlpool round: five inputs, five outputs of 0.01.
2. Ask the slide's question. (Any of five: the anonymity set.)
3. Likely question: "Can a Wasabi 2.x round hide because its amounts differ?" (It is still spotted by its size and its repeated amounts; Stütz et al.'s > 99% is for 1.x and Samourai.)

**Sources**
- @stutz_adoptionprivacycoinjoin_2022
- @svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026

:::

## Before and after the mix still leak {.smaller}

- **The mix is one transaction; the user's habits surround it.** "The traceability of addresses during the pre-mixing and post-mixing narrows down the anonymity set" [@stutz_adoptionprivacycoinjoin_2022].
- **Pre-mix:** Whirlpool first splits "any fresh input" into pool-sized outputs in a TX0 transaction [@svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026, sec. 2.1]; that transaction spends from the cluster you were tracing.
- **Address reuse:** paying a mixed output to an address already seen "directly reveals ownership by the same entity"; CoinJoin wallets avoid it, so a reuse is a user's mistake [@svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026, p. 564].
- **Post-mix:** outputs spent together after the mix undo it, by the co-spend heuristic.
- **Timing:** a large wallet that stays in the mix for many rounds stands out; knowing how long it mixes raises the odds that the outputs leaving at the end are its own [@svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026, sec. 5.3].
- **Confidence:** timing alone is Low; a reuse or post-mix co-spend is one strong line, Moderate.

[Try it: Who paid whom? (five-minute lab)](/assets/labs/who-paid-whom/index.html) · [Day 7 team game: Hide and trace](/assets/labs/hide-and-trace/index.html)

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide shows where CoinJoin users give themselves away: before the mix, after it, and by reusing addresses. It matters here because these are the leads a limits-of-tracing note lists under "what still shows". Emphasize that the leaks are behavior, so they carry the confidence of behavior.

**Key Points**
- Stütz et al.: pre-mix and post-mix traceability narrows the anonymity set.
- Svenda et al.: reusing an address directly reveals the same owner; CoinJoin wallets are built to avoid it.
- Two mixed outputs spent together later are co-spent like any other inputs.
- Svenda et al. also show that how long a large wallet keeps mixing lets an analyst give a higher probability to the outputs it withdraws.
- Course scale: timing alone is Low; a reuse or co-spend is Moderate; High needs another kind of evidence.

**Walkthrough**
1. Draw: cluster, then pre-mix split, then CoinJoin, then two outputs co-spent to one address.
2. Ask: which link survives the mix? (The post-mix co-spend: Moderate.)
3. Optional, five minutes: open the Who paid whom? lab from the link on the slide. Students predict which of five equal outputs is the ransom's, test the amounts, address types and positions, move a participants slider, meet the term anonymity set, and see unequal change amounts pair back to an input.
4. Day 7, second half of the afternoon, after the CoinJoin trace's graded note: the Hide and trace team game (about 75 minutes: briefing 10, hide 20, trace 25, reveal 20). Start it on the instructor's machine with `./lab-manager.sh start hide-and-trace` (dynamic-labs/hide-and-trace/README.md), make the teams on the instructor page, and hand each team its code. The link on the slide opens the steps each team follows. Each team hides a stolen coin in eight moves (peels, splits, merges, waits, a CoinJoin round, the mixer, cash-out), then traces another team's coin and calls each link Low, Moderate or High with its reasons. The leaks on this slide (pre-mix, reuse, post-mix co-spend, timing) are what the tracers look for.

**Sources**
- @stutz_adoptionprivacycoinjoin_2022
- @svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026

:::

## PayJoin hides a co-spend inside a payment {.smaller}

- **What it is:** a protocol "for two parties to negotiate a coinjoin transaction during a payment between them" (BIP 78) [@dorier_bip78payjoin_2019]; its status is Deployed [31 Oct 2026]{.asof}. The receiver adds an input of their own.
- **What it breaks:** the co-spend heuristic. "Because payjoin is mixing the inputs of the sender and receiver, this heuristic becomes unreliable" [@dorier_bip78payjoin_2019].
- **Why it is hard:** a PayJoin "will look like a normal transaction" [@dorier_bip78payjoin_2019]. Unlike a CoinJoin, there are no equal outputs to warn you.
- **Async PayJoin:** BIP 77 replaces the receiver's own server with an untrusted "directory server", so a receiver need not run one [@gould_bip77asyncpayjoin_2023]; its status is Draft [31 Oct 2026]{.asof}.
- **For the analyst:** this is why co-spending with no sign of a CoinJoin stays Moderate, not High.

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide introduces PayJoin, a two-party CoinJoin that looks like an ordinary payment. It matters here because it breaks the co-spend heuristic without the warning sign of equal outputs. Emphasize that it is the reason the clustering lesson's co-spend row stops at Moderate.

**Key Points**
- The CoinJoin slides ended with leaks around a mix. PayJoin breaks the same co-spend clue with no warning sign, so it belongs here. BIP 78 (2019, Deployed): sender and receiver both contribute inputs to the payment.
- The BIP itself says the common-input heuristic becomes unreliable, and the result looks like a normal transaction.
- BIP 77 (Draft): an untrusted directory server lets a receiver take PayJoins without hosting an endpoint.
- Check BIP status on the day you write.

**Walkthrough**
1. Draw a payment: two inputs, a payment output and change. Ask: one owner? (Probably; a PayJoin would make it two.)
2. Likely question: "How would I spot a PayJoin?" (Often you cannot from the chain: by design it looks like a payment. That is why co-spending stays Moderate.)

**Sources**
- @dorier_bip78payjoin_2019
- @gould_bip77asyncpayjoin_2023

:::

## Check: CoinJoin, PayJoin or a payment? {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .8em;"}

Three transactions from a ransom trace (invented data, fees left out). For each, write one line: CoinJoin, PayJoin, a payment, or something else, and what you would say about it.

| Tx | Inputs | Outputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **P** | 2: 0.04 and 0.90 BTC | 2: 0.05 and 0.89 BTC |
| **Q** | 5 inputs of 0.01 BTC, from five unrelated addresses | 5 outputs of 0.01 BTC |
| **R** | 1: 0.50 BTC, from the ransom cluster | 5 outputs of 0.10 BTC |

::: {.fragment}
**Answers.** **Q** is a CoinJoin: a repeated amount on both sides, in a Whirlpool-sized round. **R** is not a CoinJoin, because it has one input and one owner; it is a pre-mix split, and the trace continues. **P** looks like a payment, and the chain cannot rule out a PayJoin, so co-spending in it stays Moderate [@dorier_bip78payjoin_2019; @svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026].

**Part 1 in one line:** equal amounts give a CoinJoin away and PayJoin gives nothing away, so mark the first, never cluster across it, and keep co-spending at Moderate where a PayJoin cannot be ruled out.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide closes part 1 with a check every student answers. It sets three short transactions side by side and asks which is a CoinJoin, a PayJoin or a payment. It matters here because the first move on a trace is to read the transaction's shape before trusting co-spending. Emphasize that "cannot rule out" is a complete answer for P.

**Key Points**
- Q is the Whirlpool shape taught earlier: five inputs, five outputs, one repeated amount. Five owners built it, so co-spending means nothing.
- R is the trap. It has five equal outputs, but one input from one owner, so it is a split before a mix, not a mix. The 'Before and after the mix' slide called this a pre-mix split.
- P is two inputs and a payment plus change. If the receiver added an input, it is a PayJoin; the chain looks the same either way, which is why the co-spend clue stops at Moderate.
- The part's synthesis, on the slide: a CoinJoin shows, a PayJoin does not, and each changes what you do with co-spending.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the three rows. Give every student thirty seconds to write a line for each.
2. Take a show of hands on R first, because it is the most common wrong answer, then reveal all three.
3. Read the part 1 line.

**Sources**
- @dorier_bip78payjoin_2019
- @svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026

:::

## A mixer pools coins and pays out others {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

- **What it is:** FinCEN calls mixers or tumblers persons that "accept CVCs and retransmit them in a manner designed to prevent others from tracing the transmission back to its source"; such a provider "is a money transmitter" [@financialcrimesenforcementnetworkfincen_applicationcertainbusinessmodels_2019, sec. 4.5.1] [May 2019]{.asof}.
- **Custodial, on Bitcoin:** Bitcoin Fog's operator was sentenced to more than 12 years [@departmentofjustice_operatorbitcoinfog_2024]; Sinbad, sanctioned in 2023, "is believed by some industry experts to be a successor to the Blender.io mixer" [@l33_u_s_treasury_u_s_treasury_treasury_sanctions_mixer_used_by_the_dprk__2023].
- **A contract, on Ethereum:** Tornado Cash "operates on the Ethereum blockchain" [@u.s.dept.oftreasury_ustreasurysanctions_2022]. Its sanctions and delisting were covered in the lesson on VASPs and the rules.
- **For the analyst:** the coins out are not the coins in. Label the mixer, and treat each withdrawal as a new start.

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}

Nothing on the chain joins A to A': the withdrawals are grey because their owners are unknown.

```{dot}
//| echo: false
//| fig-height: 2.6
digraph Mixer {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent"];
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica"];
  subgraph cluster_inputs {
    label="Deposits";
    style=dashed;
    UserA [label="User A\n(illicit)", fillcolor="#ffdddd"];
    UserB [label="User B", fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];
    UserC [label="User C", fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];
  }
  Mixer [label="Mixer pool", shape=cylinder, fillcolor="#f5f7fb"];
  subgraph cluster_outputs {
    label="Withdrawals";
    style=dashed;
    NewA [label="A'\n(owner unknown)", fillcolor="#eeeeee"];
    NewB [label="B'", fillcolor="#eeeeee"];
    NewC [label="C'", fillcolor="#eeeeee"];
  }
  {UserA, UserB, UserC} -> Mixer -> {NewA, NewB, NewC};
}
```

:::
::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide separates a mixer from a CoinJoin: a mixer takes the coins and pays out others, so the on-chain link is cut, not hidden. It matters here because a trace into a mixer ends at the deposit, and only behavior can pick it up again. Emphasize custodial services on Bitcoin and contracts on Ethereum.

**Key Points**
- Part 1 was about one transaction several owners build together. A mixer is different: a service takes the coins and pays out others. FinCEN's 2019 guidance (sec. 4.5.1) defines an anonymizing services provider and calls it a money transmitter.
- Bitcoin Fog (sentenced 12 Nov 2024), Blender.io and Sinbad are Bitcoin mixers; Treasury's release reports that some industry experts believe Sinbad succeeded Blender.io; that is the experts' view, not the reason for the sanction.
- Tornado Cash is a set of Ethereum contracts; the lesson on VASPs and the rules covered its 2022 sanctions and 2025 delisting.
- Only User A's deposit is known to be illicit; the withdrawals are drawn grey because nothing on the chain says which one is A's. The diagram is illustrative.

**Walkthrough**
1. Point at A and A': nothing on the chain joins them.
2. Ask: what can you still say about A? (That it deposited to a labeled mixer, with the date and amount.)

**Sources**
- @financialcrimesenforcementnetworkfincen_applicationcertainbusinessmodels_2019
- @departmentofjustice_operatorbitcoinfog_2024
- @l33_u_s_treasury_u_s_treasury_treasury_sanctions_mixer_used_by_the_dprk__2023
- @u.s.dept.oftreasury_ustreasurysanctions_2022

:::

## User habits link deposit to withdrawal {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** mixers are rarely broken by their math. Wang et al. tested user habits on Tornado Cash and cut its anonymity sets by an average of 27.34% on Ethereum [@wang_zkpmixers_2023].

::: {style="font-size: .8em;"}

| Habit | What you see | Confidence alone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same address deposits and withdraws | One address on both sides of the pool | Moderate |
| Deposit and withdrawal addresses linked | A direct transfer between the two addresses | Moderate |
| Matching amounts across pools | One address's deposits in several pools match another's withdrawals, each deposit earlier | Low |
| Timing | A withdrawal soon after a deposit, in a quiet pool | Low |

: {tbl-colwidths="[30,50,20]"}

:::

The first three rows are Wang et al.'s heuristics 1, 3 and 5 [@wang_zkpmixers_2023, sec. 7.1]. Timing alone is behavior: Low on the course scale.

**Ask:** timing and matching amounts agree on one pair. Is that High?

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide lists the habits that pair a mixer deposit with a withdrawal. It matters here because these are the only routes past a mixer from the chain alone, and each carries its own confidence. Emphasize that every row is a user's mistake, not a flaw in the protocol.

**Key Points**
- The last slide ended on a pool that cuts the on-chain link. This one asks what still pairs a deposit with a withdrawal. Wang et al. (WWW 2023): five heuristics shrank Tornado Cash anonymity sets by 27.34% on average on Ethereum and 46.02% on BSC.
- H1 address reuse; H3 deposit and withdrawal addresses linked by a transfer; H5 matching totals across fixed-size pools, deposits before withdrawals.
- Timing is one of the lab's tells.
- The confidence column is the course scale, not the paper's.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read each row; ask which kind of evidence it is.
2. Ask the slide's question. (No: both are behavior from the same pool; Moderate at most.)

**Sources**
- @wang_zkpmixers_2023

:::

## Dust is bait: a dust input is not a link {.smaller}

- **The attack:** someone sends a tiny amount to an address that has already been paid, waiting for the wallet to spend it together with the owner's other coins. Bitcoin Core calls this "a serious privacy issue where a malicious user can track spends by sending small payments to a previously-paid address" [@bitcoincore_release0190_2019].
- **The defense:** Bitcoin Core 0.19 added a wallet flag, `avoid_reuse`, off by default [@bitcoincore_release0190_2019] [Nov 2019]{.asof}.
- **For the analyst, two rules:**
  - Anyone can pay any address. A tiny payment in says nothing about who sent it.
  - If the owner later spends the dust with their own coins, that co-spend is about the owner's coins, not the duster's.
- **Why it matters here:** a trace that runs through a dust input can jump to a stranger.

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide explains dusting: small unsolicited payments used to track spends. It matters here because a dust input in a trace looks like a link and is not one. Emphasize that receiving is not consent and not evidence of a relationship.

**Key Points**
- The habits slide listed what users do that links addresses. Dust is the opposite case: something done to a user that only looks like a link. The Bitcoin Core 0.19 release notes describe tracking spends with small payments to previously-paid addresses.
- The `avoid_reuse` flag (default off) keeps such coins out of later spends.
- Inbound payments prove nothing about the receiver; the receiver did not choose them.
- When dust is co-spent, the link is between the owner's coins; never extend it to the sender.

**Walkthrough**
1. Ask: an address in your trace received 0.00000600 from a sanctioned address. Is it linked? (No: anyone can send to any address.)

**Sources**
- @bitcoincore_release0190_2019

:::

## 2024: Samourai shut down, zkSNACKs stopped {.smaller}

- **24 April 2024:** FBI actions shut down Samourai's Whirlpool coordinator [@svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026, sec. 2.1]. DOJ said Whirlpool and its Ricochet feature carried "more than 80,000 Bitcoin" and "over $237 million in illegal transactions" [@irs_samouraisentenced_2025].
- **2025:** the founders pleaded guilty on 30 July [@irs_samouraiplea_2025] and were sentenced to five and four years in November [@irs_samouraisentenced_2025] [19 Nov 2025]{.asof}.
- **1 June 2024:** zkSNACKs stopped its Wasabi 2.x coordinator, "citing legal uncertainty" [@svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026, sec. 2.1].
- **After:** new coordinators took over. Wasabi 2.x mixing passed its pre-shutdown level; one coordinator, kruw.io, carries 99% of mixed inputs. A new Whirlpool coordinator started on 31 May 2025 [@svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026] [31 Oct 2026]{.asof}.
- **For the analyst:** the operators ended; the technique did not. CoinJoins "are used by both lawful and unlawful actors" [@svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026, p. 557]: a CoinJoin is a reason the trace stops, not evidence of a crime.

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide brings the CoinJoin story up to date: the two big coordinators ended in 2024, and others replaced them. It matters here because analysts will still meet Wasabi- and Whirlpool-shaped transactions dated after 2024. Emphasize dating every claim about who runs a coordinator.

**Key Points**
- Every slide so far described how the tools work. This one dates who runs them, because an analyst meets these transactions in 2025 and later. Samourai: coordinator shut down 24 Apr 2024; guilty pleas 30 Jul 2025; sentences of five years (Rodriguez, 6 Nov 2025) and four years (Hill, 19 Nov 2025).
- DOJ figures: more than 80,000 BTC through Whirlpool and Ricochet; over $237 million in illegal transactions.
- zkSNACKs (Wasabi): coordinator stopped voluntarily on 1 Jun 2024, citing legal uncertainty.
- Svenda et al.: kruw.io carries 99% of Wasabi 2.x mixed inputs; Ashigaru restarted a Whirlpool coordinator on 31 May 2025.
- A CoinJoin alone does not show criminal intent; say what it does to the trace.

**Walkthrough**
1. Ask: a Whirlpool-shaped transaction is dated 2025. Who ran the coordinator? (Not Samourai; check the date against the coordinators then running.)

**Sources**
- @svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026
- @irs_samouraisentenced_2025
- @irs_samouraiplea_2025

:::

## Check: which withdrawal links back, how sure? {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .8em;"}

A ransom cluster deposits to a labeled mixer's pool (invented data). Three withdrawals follow. For each, write one line: does it link back to the deposit, and how sure are you?

| Withdrawal | What you see |
| --- | --- |
| **W1** | Paid to the same address that made the deposit |
| **W2** | Paid four minutes after the deposit, in a pool with 200 deposits that day |
| **W3** | Address received 0.00000600 BTC from a sanctioned address a day earlier |

::: {.fragment}
**Answers.** **W1** links back: one address on both sides of the pool is a habit, so **Moderate**. **W2** is a lead only, rated **Low**, because timing is its only clue and a pool with 200 deposits that day makes a chance match likely. **W3** does not link back at all, because anyone can send dust to any address and the receiver did not choose it [@wang_zkpmixers_2023; @bitcoincore_release0190_2019].

**Part 2 in one line:** a mixer cuts the chain's link, so only a user's habits pair a deposit with a withdrawal, and each habit carries the confidence of behavior.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide closes part 2 with a check every student answers. It takes the habits table and the dust slide and asks students to rate three withdrawals from one pool. It matters here because the lab and the limits-of-tracing note both need a confidence word on each lead. Emphasize that W3 is not a weak link but no link.

**Key Points**
- W1 is the first row of the habits table: the same address deposits and withdraws. It is one strong line, so Moderate.
- W2 is the timing row. Timing alone is Low, and a pool with many deposits that day makes any single match more likely by chance.
- W3 is the dust slide's second rule: a tiny payment in says nothing about who sent it, so there is no link to rate.
- The part's synthesis, on the slide: mixers are broken by user habits, not by their math, and behavior gets a behavior confidence.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the three rows. Give every student thirty seconds to write a line for each.
2. Ask for hands on W2 (Moderate, Low or no link), then reveal.
3. Read the part 2 line.

**Sources**
- @wang_zkpmixers_2023
- @bitcoincore_release0190_2019

:::

## From raw transactions to the note's first rows {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** read the explorer, name the shape, then write the row. (Invented data, the same case as the next slide.)

```text
T7    in:  R3 (ransom cluster)  0.5003
      out: 0  0.1   1  0.1   2  0.1   3  0.1   4  0.1      fee 0.0003
J1    in:  50 inputs of 0.1 (five are T7's outputs 0-4) + one fee input 0.0005
      out: 50 outputs of 0.1                               fee 0.0005
```

1. **`T7`:** one ransom input splits into five equal outputs sized for the round, spent from the cluster: a pre-mix. The trace continues; the cluster's Moderate carries.
2. **`J1`:** 50 outputs of one repeated amount, and T7's five outputs among its inputs: a CoinJoin.
3. **Which five outputs are the ransom's?** Nothing in `J1` pairs an input with an output, so the trace stops: anonymity set 50, which five undetermined. A stop is a fact, so no confidence word.

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide derives the first two rows of the next slide's note from raw explorer output. It matters here because the lab asks students to do exactly this: read a transaction, name its shape and write a row. Emphasize the order: what the explorer shows, which rule it matches, then the row.

**Key Points**
- Parts 1 and 2 taught the shapes and the leaks; this part writes them down. `T7` is a pre-mix split, like Whirlpool's TX0 (earlier slide): one input split into equal outputs sized for the round. The 0.1 size and the 50-wide round are invented, not Whirlpool's pools. It spends from the ransom cluster, so it is still the ransom's money.
- `J1`'s 50 equal outputs are the CoinJoin shape; finding T7's five outputs among its inputs is what ties the CoinJoin to this trace.
- The stop row has no confidence word: that the CoinJoin breaks the link is what the chain shows, not a judgment.
- The fee detail is simplified; real rounds charge fees in their own ways.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read `T7` aloud: one input, five equal outputs. Ask: what shape? (A pre-mix split.)
2. Read `J1`: ask which of its outputs is the ransom's. (Undetermined: any five of 50.)
3. Point ahead: these are rows 1 and 2 of the next slide.

**Sources**
- @svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026

:::

## A limits-of-tracing note: where it stops {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** your lab product looks like this: where the trace stops, why, what still shows and how sure. (Invented data.)

::: {style="font-size: .75em;"}

| Step | What you see | The trace | Still shows | Confidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Ransom cluster splits 0.5 into five 0.1 inputs | Continues: pre-mix | The cluster entered the mix | Moderate |
| 2 | `J1`: 50 inputs, 50 outputs of 0.1 | **Stops:** CoinJoin, set of 50 | Five of the 50 outputs are the ransom's; which five is undetermined | — |
| 3 | One `J1` output pays address R7, already in the ransom cluster | Resumes for that output | Address reuse | Moderate |
| 4 | Three `J1` outputs reach one exchange deposit 10 blocks later | Lead only | Timing | Low |

: {tbl-colwidths="[7,33,22,23,15]"}

:::

The note ends at the first service, or at the stop, with the leads that remain.

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide models the lab's limits-of-tracing note on invented data. It matters here because students see the finished product before they build one. Emphasize that "undetermined" is an answer, and that each lead after the stop carries its own confidence.

**Key Points**
- The last slide derived rows 1 and 2; this one shows all four rows as the finished note. Rows 1 and 2 were derived on the previous slide.
- Step 1 inherits the cluster's Moderate from the clustering lesson.
- Step 2 is the stop: the anonymity set is 50 and nothing in the transaction picks one output.
- Step 3: address reuse is one strong line, Moderate.
- Step 4: timing alone is behavior, Low; it names a lead for an agent, not a finding.
- The data are invented; the lab uses its own captured data.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read each row left to right.
2. Ask: how would you say row 4 to an agent? ("The exchange deposit is a lead, Low: only the timing matches.")

**Sources**
- @stutz_adoptionprivacycoinjoin_2022
- @svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026

:::

## Practice: write the note for a mixer hop {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .78em;"}

The ransom cluster `R3` from the worked note pays into a mixer (invented data). Write a limits-of-tracing note: for each step, what the trace does, what still shows, and how sure you are.

| Step | What you see |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | `R3` pays 2.0 BTC to address `M1`, which one analytics platform labels a mixer |
| 2 | `M1`'s pool pays out 40 withdrawals of 0.5 BTC over two days, among them `X1` to `X4`; nothing on the chain joins the deposit to a withdrawal |
| 3 | `X2` is an address that sent 0.01 BTC into the `R3` cluster a month earlier |
| 4 | `X4`'s 0.5 BTC reaches an exchange deposit address 6 blocks later, on a day with few deposits to that exchange |

Use the four columns of the worked note: what you see, the trace, what still shows, confidence. Where the trace stops, write no confidence word.

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide asks students to write the limits-of-tracing note for a mixer hop, the same product the afternoon lab grades. It matters here because the worked note covered a CoinJoin, and a mixer stops the trace in a different way. Emphasize the four columns: they are the lab's format.

**Key Points**
- The worked note read a CoinJoin; this one reads a mixer, so students must decide where the trace stops and which leads survive, without a template for it.
- Step 1 is a deposit to a labeled mixer; the label comes from one platform, which matters for the confidence word.
- Step 2 is the stop. Step 3 is a habit link between a withdrawal address and the depositing cluster. Step 4 is timing.
- The afternoon lab asks for the same note on captured data.

**Walkthrough**
1. Remind students of the worked note's four columns and that a stop gets no confidence word.
2. Give students five minutes to write the four rows on paper or in pairs.
3. Do not reveal the answers yet; the next slide does.

**Sources**
- @wang_zkpmixers_2023

:::

## Answers: where it stops, and why {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .75em;"}

| Step | The trace | Still shows | Confidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Continues: the deposit is on the chain | `R3` paid 2.0 BTC to `M1`, with date and amount; the "mixer" label has one source | **Low** for the label: one platform's, basis unknown. The payment itself is on-chain fact and takes no word |
| 2 | **Stops:** a mixer pays out other coins | Any of the pool's 40 withdrawals could hold the ransom's 2.0 BTC; which four do is undetermined | — |
| 3 | Resumes for `X2` | A direct transfer links `X2` to the depositing cluster [@wang_zkpmixers_2023] | **Moderate:** one strong habit |
| 4 | Lead only | The exchange deposit is a name to ask about | **Low:** timing alone, in a quiet day |

: {tbl-colwidths="[7,23,45,25]"}

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide gives the answers to the practice, each with its confidence word and its reason. It matters here because hearing the reasons after trying is where students correct their own reading. Emphasize the stop row: "undetermined" is the answer, and the note is complete without a confidence word there.

**Key Points**
- Step 1 does not stop the trace; the deposit is a fact. The deposit is an on-chain fact and takes no word; the label is one platform's with its basis unknown, so Low, as the attribution lesson taught.
- Step 2 is the stop. Any of the pool's 40 withdrawals could hold the ransom, so the note says undetermined, not "probably X1".
- Step 3 is the habits table's address-link row: one strong line, Moderate, and it lets the trace resume for that one withdrawal.
- Step 4 is timing: Low, and a lead for an agent, not a finding.
- A student who wrote High on step 3 or a word on step 2 needs the habits slide again.

**Walkthrough**
1. Reveal the table after students have written their rows.
2. Read each row and ask a pair who chose a different word to say why.
3. Stress the stop row and the Low on step 4.

**Sources**
- @wang_zkpmixers_2023

:::

## Review: what still shows past the stop {.smaller}

[]{#what-to-carry-out-of-this-lesson}

::: {style="font-size: .72em;"}

**The objective:** given a trace that reaches a CoinJoin or a mixer, say where it stops, why, what still shows past the stop, and how sure you are. Answer each question from memory, then reveal.

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| **1.** Five inputs from unrelated addresses, five equal outputs: cluster across it? | [No. A CoinJoin is many owners, so mark it and stop clustering across it [@gmaxwell_coinjoinbitcoinprivacy_2013].]{.fragment} |
| **2.** A mixer pays 0.5 BTC out to four addresses after your 2.0 BTC went in: which carry the ransom? | [Undetermined: a mixer pays out other coins. Only user habits pair a deposit with a withdrawal [@wang_zkpmixers_2023].]{.fragment} |
| **3.** A withdrawal address received dust from a sanctioned address: linked? | [No. Anyone can pay any address, and the receiver did not choose it [@bitcoincore_release0190_2019].]{.fragment} |
| **4.** What does the note say where the trace stops? | [Where it stops, why, what still shows and how sure, with no confidence word on the stop itself.]{.fragment} |

: {tbl-colwidths="[45,55]"}

:::

**Next:** the privacy coins Monero and Zcash hide the trail by design, not by a tool you add. Can you now say what still shows when the trace goes dark?

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide reviews the lesson against its objective: four questions, answered from memory before each answer appears. It matters here because recalling an answer fixes it better than hearing a summary, and the questions show whether students can now do what the opening promised. Emphasize question 2: a trace that stops at a mixer is a finding, not a failure.

**Key Points**
- Question 1 returns to part 1: a CoinJoin is many owners, so co-spending fails.
- Question 2 returns to the mixer and the stop row of the practice.
- Question 3 returns to dust, the most common false link.
- Question 4 returns to the note: the stop itself carries no confidence word.
- No new facts appear here. The next lesson, on privacy coins, is named and not taught: it asks what still shows when the coin itself hides the trail.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the objective.
2. For each question, give students a few seconds to answer aloud or on paper, then reveal the answer.
3. Ask the objective as a question, then read the next-lesson line.

**Sources**
- @gmaxwell_coinjoinbitcoinprivacy_2013
- @wang_zkpmixers_2023
- @bitcoincore_release0190_2019
- @svenda_coinjoinecosystem_2026
